items.title: Centre Wellington Energy Inc. Business Case Study
Mayor Watters welcomed Ted Arnott on behalf of the Elora Festival and
notes: Elora Singers.

T. Arnott volunteer member of the Board of the Elora Festival and the Elora Singers provided a brief introduction of the 2026 program and thanked Council and the Township of Centre Wellington for their continued support.

Mark Vuorinen, Artistic Director provided an overview of the planning for the 47th annual Elora Festival which will include 3 weeks of music, 20 ticketed events, feature guest artists, outdoor concerts, unique experiences and other free events taking place throughout Centre Wellington.

He noted that the Elora Festival typically hosts approximately 4000 visitors to the area, with an estimated economic impact in 2024 of 1.2 million dollars. The festival has 110 community volunteers and the book sale which took place recently has raised approximately $80,000 for this year’s festival.
M. Vuorinen thanked Council and the Township of Centre Wellington for their continued support.

Christina Stelmacovich, Operations Manager the Elora Festival provided an update on outreach done through this organization, offering a weeklong intensive program Studio for Ensemble Singing, open to those seeking to improve their skills as a professional singer, new this year the conducting component. In addition, affiliated with the Elora Centre for the Arts, offer a Supportive Arts Program and the Circle of Song, weekly sing a long and music with residents of long-term care facilities.
C. Stelmacovich noted that they plan to expand these programs to include Elementary and Secondary Schools to help teachers and schools present choral music.

On behalf of Council, Mayor Watters thanked the Elora Festival and the Elora Singers for their presentation, and for providing Centre Wellington with a world-class festival and many years of outstanding entertainment.

items.title: Tova Davidson, Executive Director on behalf of Sustainable Waterloo
notes: Region (SWR) provided an update for 2025, it was a year of scaling, expanding into new geographies and supporting 40 communities.

She noted SWR started as a student project almost 18 years ago and has continued to grow into several programs including the Climate action program whole community action plan, designing how we move forward together to create low carbon futures that drive towards equity, inclusion, resiliency and prosperity. In addition to Waterloo Region, SWR now serves Guelph-Wellington, Perth, Oxford and Dufferin Counties and scaled across the county by creation of another non-profit “Green Economy Canada” supporting other non-profits across Canada to create the Impact network Program.

T. Davidson provided a brief overview of the programs run by SWR, the organics program has been operating in Centre Wellington for some time formally run by the circular innovation council, taking the organic waste and bringing it to an anaerobic digester making it into clean energy, also offer food rescue as part of this program, the impact network program which Centre Wellington is a member, helps organizations track their carbon footprint and assists with tracking the carbon footprint for events.

She commented on evolve1 Canada’s first net positive energy office building build by The Cora Group. Last year SWR launched the Frameworks program, Ontario’s only building innovation exchange designed to support the building and development sector with building retrofits and in preparation for the projected harmonized code in 2030.

SWR launched a “microforest” program, native species trees in urban spaces, planted in school yards parks and other areas benefitting the community. The microforest program is projected to have planted 75 forests by the end of 2026.

T. Davidson responded to questions and comments from Council regarding requirements for development of microforests, the associated costs and the opportunity to attend SWR’s pretty spaces, geothermal tours and SWR’s position on advocating for Provincial policy.

notes: Councillor Lustgarten‑Evoy provided an update on the OSUM Conference held in Parry Sound. Three councillors from Centre Wellington attended the conference. Councillor Lustgarten‑Evoy also shared that she is honoured to represent Centre Wellington as a member of the OSUM Executive.

Councillor MacDonald shared an update on Safe Communities, highlighting the launch of the Ontario Students Against Drunk Driving (OSAID) campaign. She also noted the continued popularity of the Seniors Committee bus tours, which consistently sell out, most recently for a trip to a Blue Jays game.

Councillor Wilton, on behalf of herself and Councillor Adams, shared that the Healthy Communities Advisory Committee met last week. Members received a preview of the upcoming transit study, Township of Centre Wellington is exploring expanded public transit options and update was also provided on the Water Softener Replacement Program, which aims to support the Township’s water system by replacing older units with more efficient models.

items.title: Randy Vaine spoke on behalf of Royal Canadian Legion - Fergus and
notes: Elora Branches on the proposed cross walk policy.

R. Vaine stated that in 2025, the Royal Canadian Legion, Fergus and Elora Branches requested that the Township install veterans’ crosswalks in Elora and Fergus. There are currently over 110 veterans’ crosswalks across Canada. These crosswalks are typically installed near cenotaphs and Royal Canadian Legion Branches to honour veterans and active service members, and they act as a permanent, year-round community tribute.
He noted that Veterans should not be lumped into a group as part of a policy. These men and women fought for Canada and for freedom.
Thousands of Canadian veterans have died or been injured while fighting for the freedoms and the lifestyle that Canadians enjoy today.

items.title: Don Cubbidge, President of the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 229 in
notes: Elora, spoke in opposition to the Township staff’s recommendation not to install veterans’ crosswalks. Provided a brief overview of the Act of Remembrance which happens across the Township and the Country every November 11th, where the local branches organize and conduct Remembrance Day services at their respective cenotaphs, it’s a solemn occasion and an opportunity for the community to pay their respect to those who made the ultimate sacrifice. Branch 229 has been conducting these services since 1932.

He noted that the veterans’ crosswalks are not the same, as they are meant to honour veterans every day, not just November 11th. They recognize both past and current veterans, these veterans are neighbours, coworkers, and friends in the community.

D. Cubbidge provided a brief presentation and commented that he provided a mock up of what the cross walks could look like at a DEI meeting in 2025, the mock-up is in line with the standards of the Royal Canadian Legion.

items.title: Randy Graham, President Royal Canadian Legion Branch 275 Fergus,
notes: spoke on behalf of the members and executive, echoing the thoughts of D. Cubbidge, the staff recommendation to not allow veterans’ crosswalks is not the right path to take in light of the debt owed to those who paid the ultimate sacrifice for the rights and freedoms Canadians have today.

He stated that today we have annual remembrance services in the form of cenotaph services, dinners, parades and student literary competitions and stressed that remembrance is every day. Veterans’ crosswalks provide a daily reminder of what men and women in the service do for us every day. Communities all around Centre Wellington have already approved and installed veterans’ crosswalks, our community is proud, progressive, and thankful for service, and we need to continually demonstrate this to our citizens and veterans.
R. Graham thanked Council and commented that this is the 100th Anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion and respectfully requested that Council see this as timely and move forward.
Mayor Watters asked if there were any questions or comments from Council, a brief discussion ensued.

motions.text: WHEREAS generations of Canadians have served our country and the world during times of war, military conflict, and peace. Through their courage and sacrifice, these men and women have helped to ensure that we live in freedom and peace, while also fostering freedom and peace around the world; and WHEREAS every year on November 11, Canadians pause in a silent moment of remembrance for the men and women who have served, and continue to serve our country during times of war, conflict, and peace; and WHEREAS the Royal Canadian Legion’s mission to promote remembrance is a yearlong commitment, they endeavor to promote it through programs, services, and resources; and WHEREAS the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 's in Elora and Fergus has locally promoted the objectives of the Royal Canadian Legion’s mission since 1952; and WHEREAS the Township of Centre Wellington has previously partnered with the Royal Canadian Legion which displays memorial banners, wreaths, and flags to honour veterans, past and present, that served to protect our peace and freedom; and WHEREAS municipalities such as Town of Bradford West Gwillimbury, City of Calgary, City of Belleville and Municipality of Chatham-Kent, Wellington North, New Hamburg, Guelph, Halton Hills have installed Veterans’ Crosswalks to provide a year-round reminder of the sacrifices made by veterans and their families to keep our communities safe. THEREFORE, BE IT RESOLVED that Staff be directed to report back to Council with costs and initiate the crosswalk installed before Remembrance Day November 11, 2026. THEREFORE, BE IT FINALLY RESOLVED that the Staff Report includes information on the feasibility of the Veterans’ Crosswalk being located in Elora, and Fergus in the Municipality of Centre Wellington and Wellington County.
